test_text.title: Why fairy tales are really scary tales

article.title: Why fairy tales are really scary tales
glossary: * Folklorists: those who study traditional stories

items.sentence_raw: People of every culture tell each other fairy tales but the same story often takes a variety of forms in different parts of the world.
items.explain: Q27: The passage says *'the same story often takes a variety of forms in different parts of the world'* — **'a variety of forms'** means the plot details change from place to place. This matches option **C**: *'show considerable global variation'*. So the answer is **C**.

items.sentence_raw: In the story of "Little Red Riding Hood" that European children are familiar with, a young girl on the way to see her grandmother meets a wolf and tells him where she is going.
The wolf runs on ahead and disposes of the grandmother, then gets into bed dressed in the grandmother's clothes to wait for Little Red Riding Hood.
You may think you know the story - but which version?
In some versions, the wolf swallows up the grandmother, while in others it locks her in a cupboard.
In some stories Red Riding Hood gets the better of the wolf on her own, while in others a hunter or a woodcutter hears her cries and comes to her rescue.

The universal appeal of these tales is frequently attributed to the idea that they contain cautionary messages: in the case of "Little Red Riding Hood", to listen to your mother, and avoid talking to strangers.
"It might be what we find interesting about this story is that it's got this survival-relevant information in it," says anthropologist Jamie Tehrani at Durham University in the UK.
But his research suggests otherwise.
"We have this huge gap in our knowledge about the history and prehistory of storytelling, despite the fact that we know this genre is an incredibly ancient one," he says.
That hasn't stopped anthropologists, folklorists* and other academics devising theories to explain the importance of fairy tales in human society.
items.explain: Q29: The passage says academics kept *'devising theories'* even without proof — **'devising theories'** means creating ideas. Option **F** says these theories *'have been developed without factual basis'*, which matches the idea that they were made despite a *'huge gap in our knowledge'*. So the answer is **F**.

items.sentence_raw: Now Tehrani has found a way to test these ideas, borrowing a technique from evolutionary biologists.
items.explain: Q30: Tehrani found a way to test ideas by *'borrowing a technique from evolutionary biologists'* — **'borrowing a technique'** means using their methods. Option **A** says insights *'may be provided through methods used in biological research'*, which is a direct match. So the answer is **A**.

items.sentence_raw: To work out the evolutionary history, development and relationships among groups of organisms, biologists compare the characteristics of living species in a process called 'phylogenetic analysis'.
Tehrani has used the same approach to compare related versions of fairy tales to discover how they have evolved and which elements have survived longest.
Tehrani's analysis focused on "Little Red Riding Hood" in its many forms, which include another Western fairy tale known as "The Wolf and the Kids".
items.explain: Q37: The passage says Tehrani's analysis *'focused on "Little Red Riding Hood" in its many forms'* — **'many forms'** means he looked at different versions of the same basic story. Option **B** says he *'looked at many different forms of the same basic story'*, which is a perfect match. So the answer is **B**.

items.sentence_raw: Checking for variants of these two tales and similar stories from Africa, East Asia and other regions, he ended up with 58 stories recorded from oral traditions.
items.explain: Q31: All 58 stories Tehrani analysed were *'recorded from oral traditions'* — **'oral traditions'** means they were spoken, not written down. Option **E** says they *'were originally spoken rather than written'*, which is exactly what the passage tells us. So the answer is **E**.

items.sentence_raw: Once his phylogenetic analysis had established that they were indeed related, he used the same methods to explore how they have developed and altered over time.
items.explain: Q32: Tehrani's analysis first *'established that they were indeed related'* — **'related'** means there are family connections or **links** between the stories. The summary asks if **links** existed among the 58 stories, and the passage confirms they did. So the answer is **D**.

items.sentence_raw: First he tested some assumptions about which aspects of the story alter least as it evolves, indicating their importance.
items.explain: Q33: He tested which aspects *'alter least as it evolves'* — **'alter least'** means they have the fewest changes or **variations**. The summary asks which aspects had fewest **variations**, and the passage says he was looking for the parts that change the least. So the answer is **F**.

items.sentence_raw: Folklorists believe that what happens in a story is more central to the story than the characters in it - that visiting a relative, only to be met by a scary animal in disguise, is more fundamental than whether the visitor is a little girl or three siblings, or the animal is a tiger instead of a wolf.
However, Tehrani found no significant difference in the rate of evolution of incidents compared with that of characters.
"Certain episodes are very stable because they are crucial to the story, but there are lots of other details that can evolve quite freely," he says.
items.explain: Q34: Tehrani found that *'certain episodes are very stable... but there are lots of other details that can evolve quite freely'* — **'episodes'** are the **events** in the story. The summary says some **events** tended to change over time, which matches the *'details that can evolve quite freely'*. So the answer is **B**.

items.sentence_raw: Neither did his analysis support the theory that the central section of a story is the most conserved part.
He found no significant difference in the flexibility of events there compared with the beginning or the end.
But the really big surprise came when he looked at the cautionary elements of the story.
items.explain: Q35: The *'really big surprise'* came when he looked at the *'cautionary elements'* — **'cautionary'** means giving a **warning**. The summary asks about parts that provide a **warning**, and the passage says these were surprisingly unimportant. So the answer is **C**.

items.sentence_raw: "Studies on hunter-gatherer folk tales suggest that these narratives include really important information about the environment and the possible dangers that may be faced there - stuff
that's relevant to survival," he says.
Yet in his analysis such elements were just as flexible as seemingly trivial details.
items.explain: Q28: Tehrani found that cautionary elements were *'just as flexible as seemingly trivial details'* — **'flexible'** here means they change easily, so they are NOT the reason stories survive. This directly rejects the idea that useful lessons are the reason for survival, which is option **B**. So the answer is **B**.

items.sentence_raw: What, then, is important enough to be reproduced from generation to generation?
The answer, it would appear, is fear - blood-thirsty and gruesome aspects of the story, such as the eating of the grandmother by the wolf, turned out to be the best preserved of all.
items.explain: Q36: The best-preserved aspect was *'fear - blood-thirsty and gruesome aspects'* — **'gruesome'** and **'blood-thirsty'** are all about **horror**. The summary says the most important aspect for survival was **horror**, which matches the passage exactly. So the answer is **G**.

items.sentence_raw: Why are these details retained by generations of storytellers, when other features are not?
Tehrani has an idea: "In an oral context, a story won't survive because of one great teller.
It also needs to be interesting when it's told by someone who's not necessarily a great storyteller."
Maybe being swallowed whole by a wolf, then cut out of its stomach alive is so gripping that it helps the story remain popular, no matter how badly it's told.
Jack Zipes at the University of Minnesota, Minneapolis, is unconvinced by Tehrani's views on fairy tales.
"Even if they're gruesome, they won't stick unless they matter," he says.
items.explain: Q38: Jack Zipes says *'Even if they're gruesome, they won't stick unless they matter'* — **'won't stick'** means they won't survive, and **'matter'** means they have a deeper significance. Option **D** says features *'only survive if they have a deeper significance'*, which is exactly what Zipes believes. So the answer is **D**.

items.sentence_raw: He believes the perennial theme of women as victims in stories like "Little Red Riding Hood" explains why they continue to feel relevant.
But Tehrani points out that although this is often the case in Western versions, it is not always true elsewhere.
In Chinese and Japanese versions, often known as "The Tiger Grandmother", the villain is a woman, and in both Iran and Nigeria, the victim is a boy.
items.explain: Q39: Tehrani points out that in Chinese and Japanese versions, *'the villain is a woman, and... the victim is a boy'* — this directly contradicts Zipes' idea that the theme is always about *'women as victims'*. Tehrani uses these examples to show Zipes' theory is wrong, which is option **A**. So the answer is **A**.

items.sentence_raw: Mathias Clasen at Aarhus University in Denmark isn't surprised by Tehrani's findings.
"Habits and morals change, but the things that scare us, and the fact that we seek out entertainment that's designed to scare us - those are constant," he says.
Clasen believes that scary stories teach us what it feels like to be afraid without having to experience real danger, and so build up resistance to negative emotions.
items.explain: Q40: Clasen believes scary stories *'teach us what it feels like to be afraid without having to experience real danger'* — this means they are a safe way to learn about fear. Option **A** says *'They are a safe way of learning to deal with fear'*, which matches this idea perfectly. So the answer is **A**.

subtitles: Some people think that fairy tales are just stories to amuse children, but their universal and enduring appeal may be due to more serious reasons
